For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the tea came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

## What counts as tea

<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-tea" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-tea-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of tea, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

<a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach tea

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach tea comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Tea, as sold from unspiked sample, GF-AAS had cadmium higher at 560 µg/kg, against 530 µg/kg for unspiked sample, MSPME-FAAS in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dehghani Zahra, Dadfarnia Shayessteh, Haji Shabani Ali Mohammad, Ehrampoush Mohammad Hassan · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Magnetic Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes Modified with Polythiophene as a Sorbent for Simultaneous Solid Phase Microextraction of Lead and Cadmium from Water and Food Samples</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.



<a id="ranges-by-source-region-and-variety"></a>
## Which forms and regions measured lower

<a id="hmi-ing-013"></a>

Ma · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/deoliveira2018-traditional-herbal-teas-metals">Metal concentrations in traditional and herbal teas and their potential risks to human health</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/deoliveira2018-traditional-herbal-teas-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO GEMS/Food submissions reported lead in tea, dried from 6,382 results in 3 reporting regions, with subgroup medians from 17.7 to 950 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-tea" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-tea" data-question="How do heavy metals get into tea?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into tea?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, tea from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than tea from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dehghani Zahra, Dadfarnia Shayessteh, Haji Shabani Ali Mohammad, Ehrampoush Mohammad Hassan · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Magnetic Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes Modified with Polythiophene as a Sorbent for Simultaneous Solid Phase Microextraction of Lead and Cadmium from Water and Food Samples</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Tea, as sold from unspiked sample, MSPME-FAAS had lead higher at 5,620 µg/kg, against 5,580 µg/kg for unspiked sample, GF-AAS in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Dehghani Zahra, Dadfarnia Shayessteh, Haji Shabani Ali Mohammad, Ehrampoush Mohammad Hassan · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Magnetic Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes Modified with Polythiophene as a Sorbent for Simultaneous Solid Phase Microextraction of Lead and Cadmium from Water and Food Samples</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/dehghani2020-food-lead-cadmium-mspe">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-types-of-tea-have-the-lowest-levels" data-anchor="which-types-of-tea-have-the-lowest-levels" data-question="Which types of tea have the lowest levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which types of tea have the lowest levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

For lead, the HMI reference median was lowest for tea, dried (410 µg/kg) and highest for tea, as sold (450 µg/kg); forms differ in water content, so this compares foods as sold or eaten, not uptake.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/deoliveira2018-traditional-herbal-teas-metals|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Letuzia M. de Oliveira, Suchismita Das, Evandro B. da Silva, Peng Gao, Julia Gress, Yungen Liu, Lena Q. Ma · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/deoliveira2018-traditional-herbal-teas-metals">Metal concentrations in traditional and herbal teas and their potential risks to human health</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Science of the Total Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/deoliveira2018-traditional-herbal-teas-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-tea" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-tea" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in tea?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in tea?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, tea, dried had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (17.7 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (950 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EURO (20 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (40 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-tea" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-tea" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in tea?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in tea?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same tea.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Tea, dried (EURO) had lead equal to at 200 µg/kg, against 200 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (tea, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-tea-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-tea-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in tea is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in tea is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 15 results from 4 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fera2015-uk-tds-metals|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Baxter M, Brereton N · 2015</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fera2015-uk-tds-metals">Total Diet Study of metals and other elements in food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food and Environment Research Agency report for the UK Food Standards Agency, Fera report 15/06, project FS102081</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fera2015-uk-tds-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|19]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">The First Hong Kong Total Diet Study: Inorganic Arsenic</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Centre for Food Safety, Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 7.9 µg/kg (mean) in tea, dried from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source
